Many members of this group were associated with the Cult of Sabazios, which was mocked by Aristophanes and later became popular in Athens, and members of this group were given a tax called the xenikon telos to be able to sell goods. This group became obsolete by the adoption of the paroikoi distinction, and members of this group operated under a supervisor known as a prostates. Some members of this group were granted isoteleia, or equal rights, and members of this group could only be granted citizenship if offered by the city. Identify this social class of ancient Greece, comprised of residents in a polis who did not have citizenship rights.

After this battle, the winning side plundered the camp of the losers and created a bronze column of intertwining snakes called the "tripod" of this battle. Engagements in this battle included the cavalry charge of Masistius against Olympiodorus, and the losing side of this battle camped at the Asopus River. This battle saw the participation of Aristodemus, one of the two survivors of Thermopylae, and according to tradition this battle occurred on the same day as Mycale. Including the death of the Persian general Mardonius, identify this victory for Pausanias in 479 B.C. Which ended the land conflict in the Persian Wars.

The columns of this building were taken from Mons Claudianus in Egypt, and this building was constructed around the same time as the nearby Saepta Julia. Excavated by Rodolfo Lanciani, the original version of this building may have faced the opposite direction. The very top of this building contains a feature known as the oculus, and this building's inscription references its constructor, Marcus Agrippa. Rebuilt by Hadrian, identify this building in Rome famous for its opening, a domed temple originally dedicated to all the gods.

One author of this name wrote about Julius Caesar's campaigns in Gaul in the poem Bellum Sequanum and completed a translation of the Argonautica Â– that figure was from Atax. The more famous author with this name wrote a work which examined archaic words found in the works of Plautus, and in addition to Questions of Plautus he wrote three books on farming in Rerum Rusticarum. That author was from Reate and first recorded Rome's founding date as April 21, 753 B.C. This author may be better known for his 150 books of Menippean satires and twenty-five book treatise dedicated to Cicero titled On the Latin Language. Identify this prolific writer called the "most learned of all Romans" by Quintillian.

This figure dreamt that his son was killed by a spear, and later that son Atys was accidentally killed by his bodyguard Adrastus while hunting a boar. In another story about this figure, a visitor cited Tellus and Biton and Cleobis as the happiest people in the world. After consulting the Delphic Oracle, this son of Alyattes was told that a mighty empire would fall if he crossed the Halys River, which backfired and led to his capture in Sardis. Known for receiving a visit from Solon, identify this wealthy king of Lydia.

One part of this event involved the eating of the mustaceum, and at the end of this event onlookers would yell "Talassio" and sing Fescennine Verses. One participant in this event wore a "knot of Hercules" and used a spear to part her hair into six sections, and this event included the chanting of the phrase "Quando tu Gaius, ego Gaia." Types of these events included coemptio and confarreatio, and one of these events between two slaves was known as a contubernium. Identify these events in Rome which featured a pronuba, or matron of honor, in addition to a bride and groom.

This region was home to the Trinovantes who were led by the king Mandubracius, and one rebellion in this region ended when Allectus murdered Carausius. Venutius deposed his former wife Cartimandua to rule part of this region, and governors of this region included Ostorious Scapula and Aulus Plautius. This region was the site of the Battle of Mons Graupius, and the Battle of Watling Street took place between Suetonius Paulinus and the revolting wife of Prasutagus here. Identify this region of the Roman empire associated with Agricola and the revolt of Boudicca, the site of Hadrian's Wall.

In ancient Rome, members of this occupation were registered by the Aediles in the vectigal meretricium, and supposedly Claudius's wife Valeria Messalina engaged in a contest with a member of this occupation. They were encouraged to die their hair yellow, red, or blue and often wore bright togas, and a holiday celebrating this occupation was Floralia. Members of this occupation worked under a leno, and the term for them was lupa, which could also refer to a she-wolf. Identify this occupation in ancient Rome consisting of women who usually worked in brothels.

In T.S. Eliot's The Wasteland, the author recalls, "Stetson! You who were with me in the ships" of this battle at the end of "The Burial of the Dead." The winning commander of this battle was given a torch-bearer and a flute-player to accompany him at all times. This victory was inspired by success at the Battle of Agrigentum and reversed an earlier loss at the Lipari Islands. This battle was a victory over Hannibal Gisgo, and it saw the first Roman use of the corvus by the winning commander Gaius Duillius. Identify this 260 B.C. Battle off the coast of northern Sicily, the first naval victory for the Romans in the First Punic War.

These structures were constructed with the help of tools called chorobates and they began at places called castella. Constructed with volcanic pozzuolana, closely related structures called "leats" were often built in Britain. Intact remains of these structures can be found in Nimes, France and Segovia, Spain. The Anio Novus stretched the furthest from the city, and the first one was constructed in 312 B.C. By Appius Claudius Caecus. Identify these Roman structures used to transport water above ground.

Officials who participated in this event included the purple-robed Hellanodikai, and prophecies were interpreted by members of the Lamides and Klytiades families. Participants in this event took oaths before the statue of Zeus Horkios, and during this event participants proceeded from the Prytaneion to the Altis. There, one hundred oxen would be sacrificed before the dolichos, diaulos, and stadion took place. Statues of Zeus at this event's site were funded by the fines levied to cheaters during this event. Identify this festival established in 776 B.C. In its namesake location, the chief of the Greek games held in honor of Zeus.

This father of Oxyntas participated in the siege if Numantia, and this figure once remarked that Rome was a "city for sale." This figure came to power following the death of Micipsa in which he killed Hiempsal and drove out Adherbal. This ruler fought against a force led by Calpurnius Bestia and later against a force under Caecilius Metellus. This ruler's father-in-law Bocchus turned him over to the Romans, after he started a conflict by massacring Italian citizens at Circa, identify this ruler handed over to Sulla, a king of Numidia in the late 2nd century B.C.

This author wrote a defense of classical religion which debunked claims of Manetho and the title Egyptian writer in his "Against Apion." This author was influenced by the Universal History of Nicolas of Damascus, and one of this author's works is a twenty-one book historiography written for wealthy patrons. This author wrote another work in Aramaic which features events such as the siege of Masada. The author of The Antiquities of the Jews and The Jewish War, identify this Greek who wrote in Hebrew, the primary classical Jewish historian.

This figure was allegedly prosecuted by Hermippus on charges of impiety, and this figure was blamed for being responsible for the Samian War, and in The Acharnians Aristophanes blamed this figure for starting the Peloponnesian War. Later involved with Lysicles, this figure was accused by some of being a harlot, and this figure's only son was one of the six executed for not picking up survivors following the Battle of Arginusae. Identify this woman from Miletus who became an important figure in Athenian politics by being the unmarried companion of Pericles.

This modern day nation is the home of a huge gate called the Porta Nigra, and was the site of the dense Hercynian Forest. Ancient cities in this nation include Mogontiacum and Aquae Mattiacorum, and the leader of the Batavian Rebellion settled in Colonia Agrippina in this modern nation. Diocletian chose one of his capitals at this nation's city of Augusta Treverorum. Caesar famously bridged one river in this modern day nation in just ten days. Identify this modern days nation which contains the Rhine River and the cities of Mainz, Wiesbaden, and Cologne.

According to Livy, this ruler cut off the heads of the tallest poppies while talking to a messenger in a garden, which allowed his son to know how to conquer Gabii. This ruler allied with Aristodemus of Cumae and Octavius Mamillus, and he sought the help of the king of Clusium. This ruler purchased only three of the original nine Sibylline Books, and his son Aruns killed Lucius Iunius Brutus in battle. His son's rape of Lucretia led to his expulsion and subsequent alliance with Lars Porsenna. Identify this figure driven from Rome in 510 B.C., the seventh and last king of Rome.

At one point in this conflict, one ruler chose to remain in Sicily rather than take an offer from King Ceraunus. One envoy in this conflict was Cineas, and this conflict saw an attempt to bribe the Roman ambassador Gaius Fabricius. This war began from a broken treaty between Thurii and Tarentum, and early battles in this war occurred at Heraclea and Asculum. The losing commander in this conflict was eventually killed by a roof tile during a street fight in Argos, and he was expelled from Italy after a loss to Curius Dentatus at the Battle of Beneventum. Identify this 280 to 275 B.C. Conflict against a king of Epirus, whose wins at high costs became known as his namesake "victories."

This author adapted some of his old rhetorical exercises into the essays On the Malice of Herodotus and On the Virtue of Alexander. He served as a priest at Delphi, and wrote a work which contained many essays including "Roman Questions," and "Greek Questions." In addition to writing Moralia, this author is more famous for a work that begins with a discussion of Epaminondas and Scipio Africanus and contains comparisons of Theseus and Romulus and Pyrrhus and Marius. Identify this Greek author and biographer who authored Parallel Lives.

Standards for the study of this system was adopted in 1961 in the Wingspread Convention, and Emmett Bennett devised a scheme for numbering and cataloging this system. Alice Kober studied this system while a student of Sir John Myres, and this system used vertical lines to separate words and didn't distinguish between stops. It was finally deciphered in 1953 by John Chadwick and Michael Ventris long after the discovery of many tablets by Sir Arthur Evans. Identify this language used for writing Mycenaean Greek.

This man first came to prominence by serving as strategos for the Antiochis at the Battle of Marathon, and this son of Lysimachus led a force which took out a Persian garrison at Psyttaleia during the Battle of Salamis. This man was responsible for fixing the tax rate levied on members of the Delian League as the treasurer of Athens, and he was recalled out of his ostracism after just three years. In one story, this figure helped an illiterate farmer fill out his ballot for that ostracism, and when asked the reason the farmer replied that he was tired of hearing this man's nickname. Identify this lifelong rival to Themistocles, whose steadiness and moral upstanding led him to be called "the Just."

According to Pliny, a man from Cadiz walked all the way to Rome just to get a glimpse of this author, and then immediately journeyed back. Asinius Pollio criticized this author for a rustic style which he called patavinitas after this author's home city of Padua. This author's major work was condensed into chapter summaries called periochae. This author's major work ends with Drusus the Elder and contained a total of 142 books, 35 of which are still extant. Identify this golden age Roman historian who wrote Ab Urbe Condita.

It isn't Valens, but this Roman emperor fought and won at Adrianople as part of a campaign which included victories at the Battle of the Hellespont and the Battle of Chrysopolis. This man killed his wife Fausta and his oldest son Crispus, and his reforms included disbanding the Praetorian Guard. This emperor was succeeded by his three sons who split the empire, and he convened the Council of Nicaea and issued the Edict of Milan. Coming to power after defeating Maxentius at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge, identify this figure whose deathbed conversion allowed him to become the first Christian Roman emperor.

This author wrote of the culinary commentaries of Archestratus of Gela in his Hedyphagetica, and he wrote of the universe and theology in his Epicharmus and Euhemerus. This author wrote of his travels with Fulvius Nobilior in the drama Ambracia, and this uncle of Pacuvius wrote that he had three hearts due to his knowledge of Latin, Greek, and Oscan. This author wrote a tragedy based on the rape of the Sabine women, but this author's most famous work was an eighteen book history down to the time of Cato the Elder that was the first Latin poem to adopt dactylic hexameter as its meter. Identify this Calabrian author of the Annales.

The eventual loser of this battle made a funeral pyre from wagons for him to kill himself in case he were taken prisoner, and the primary account of this battle came from Jordanes. One participant in this battle, Thorismund, accidentally came home to the wrong camp, and was the son of the slain king Theodoric. The loser of this battle had earlier demanded his marriage to Honoria, while is winner is sometimes known as "The Last Roman." A victory for Flavius Aetius, identify this 451 battle against Attila the Hun, perhaps Rome's last military action.

This figure's grandfather was a tyrant from Sicyon who renamed the tree traditional tribes as hyatai, oneatai, and choireatai, or "pig-people," "ass-people," and "swine-people." This figure and his family were exiled after Isagoras appealed to Cleomenes I, but he was later recalled and divided the population into ten demes based on three trittyes which consisted of people from the city, coast, and inland. This man expanded the Boule to five hundred members, and he is sometimes crediting with establishing the practice of ostracism. Identify this figure whose reforms around 508 B.C. Led him to be called the "Father of Athenian Democracy."

This work ends with an alliance made with the Spartan leader Thibron, and toward the end of this work many of the characters are employed by Seuthes II in Thrace. In one episode from this work, an army cried "thalassa, thalassa" after reaching Trebizond and viewing the ocean, and the plot was set into motion when generals including Clearchus were killed by Tissaphernes. Recounting a victory for Artaxerxes II at the 401 Battle of Cunaxa, identify this work that catalogued the journey of the Ten Thousand, a work by Xenophon.

This geographical feature was visited by the admiral Himilco, who noted that its nearby "Muddy Sea" contained "great monsters" which "swim languidly among the sluggishly creeping ships." This name of this feature may have referred to a nearby Temple of Melqart, and this feature was associated with locations called Abyla and Calpe. This feature bore the motto "ne plus ultra" and according to Plato, the kingdom of Atlantis lay just beyond this feature. Identified with the modern Rock of Gibraltar, identify these giant rocks that mark the entrance to the Mediterranean Sea, named for a certain Greek hero.

The first of these conflicts was won by an army under Publius Rupilius. One of these conflicts was fought against Salvius, who took the name "King Tryphon," and was assisted by Athenion, and the first of these was started by Eunus and Cleon in Sicily. The most notable of these conflicts featured the generals Crixus and Oenomaus, and its surviving participants were crucified along the Appian Way. Identify this series of three conflicts in the 2nd and 1st century B.C., the third of which was put down by Crassus and started by the revolt of Spartacus, in which members of a certain social class rebelled against Roman armies.

According to Frontinus, these events were made possible in Rome because of surpluses from the Trans Tiberim gardens, which was supplied by the Aqua Alsietina. These events were prepared by opening the hypogeum and filling it, and sides in these events were led by the navis praetoria. One of these features 19,000 convicts and was held by Claudius in the Fucine Lake. Often taking place in the Colosseum after it was filled with water, identify this special type of combat which reenacted certain events taking place between ships.

One side in this battle chose to march through Thisbae and took the fortress at Creusis rather than taking the usual route, and at one point during this battle Jason of Pherae persuaded a force under Archidamus III not to march into certain defeat. The winning general of this battle used an "oblique infantry" formation which led to the death of the opposing king Cleombrotus I, and this battle occurred nine years before a second engagement between the two sides at Mantinea. Identify this 371 B.C. Victory in Boeotia of Epaminondas and the Thebans over the forces of Sparta.

One early temple in this location contained a sculpture of a three-headed serpent and was called the "bluebeard" temple. Buildings in this location's vicinity include the Theatre of Herodes Atticus and the Pandroseion. One building in this place has a portico with six caryatids, and another building in this location featured columns with an entasis, or curve, and was built by Ictinus and Callicrates. Identify this home to the Erechtheum and the Parthenon, the citadel of Athens that literally means "high city."

One component of this event was the exchange of small earthenware figurines called sigillaria, and the an image of the honoree of this event was present in a meal called the lectisternium. During this event's feast a Lord of Misrule was chosen and people wore a synthesis and pilleus rather than a toga. Slaves were treated as equals and waited on during this event, and gambling was made legal for the duration of this event. Identify this week long holiday starting December 17, the Roman equivalent of Christmas which honored the divine father of Jupiter.

This city was home to the rebellion of Domitius Alexander during the reign of Maxentius, and Cappelianus defeated Gordian I and Gordian II in a battle at this city during the year of the six emperors. The Lex Rubria established a colony at this city known as Junonia, and this city was made the capital of the Vandal Kingdom by Gaiseric. Home to Tertullian, this city became a Roman outpost after an army under Scipio Aemilianus destroyed it and salted the earth. Identify this African city which was the center of an empire that waged the Punic Wars against Rome.

The broad power implied by this decision was later narrowed in the case of Reid v. Covert. If the power arising from this decision directly contravenes state law, the instrument upon which the power is founded must be self-executing, or state law trumps. Much to the delight of Jeff Hoppes, this case arose from the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, which the plaintiff alleged violated the Tenth Amendment. Name this case that held that a treaty may give the federal government powers that it would otherwise not have the constitutional power to exercise, whose plaintiff was a midwestern state.

The actions at the center of this case arose after the victim came back from South America and the perpetrator was not civilly committed by Dr. Moore. Bengal native Prosenjit Poddar strangled the daughter of Russian immigrants, giving rise to this civil case. Name this case in which a UC-Berkeley student was murdered by a stalker who had previously confessed his desire to kill her to his psychiatrist, in which the court established that the duty to warn trumped doctor-patient confidentiality.
Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California

A "discovery group" named after this man was the plaintiff in a law of finders case in which that group claimed that gold found in a shipwreck in 1857 was their property because it was abandoned. The Harvard professor who is much-beloved for creating the modern case method of law school took his first and middle names from this person and had the surname Langdell. The legitimate claim of right in the case of Johnson v. M'Intosh was traced back to this man's actions, which included a landing at San Salvador. Name this Genoese guy who discovered America.

The McLaurin case ended one application of this doctrine, which also undermined in the Clark doll test. This doctrine was applied in the case of Sweatt v. Painter, which held that it would require the University of Texas to construct a second law library. Name this doctrine promulgated in Plessy and overturned in Brown v. Board of Education.

This case centered on a theory of wrongdoing based on parallel conduct. One commonly cited line from this decision mentions "nudging across the line." This case arose from an alleged secretive price-fixing agreement in violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act. Name this case, extended in Iqbal v. Ashcroft, which reinterpreted Conley to hold that a complaint must state facts that raise the plaintiff's right to relief about a speculative level.

According to Wikipedia, and corroborated elsewhere, reading this case inspired William Gaddis to write A Frolic of His Own. Judge Andrews wrote this opinion's notable dissent. This opinion, which all law students should know begins by describing the plaintiff's attempts to venture to Rockaway Beach, held that the defendant only owed a duty to a foreseeable plaintiff after a package carrying a shit-ton of fireworks fell onto electrified tracks and exploded, causing a fracas. Name this torts case in which Cardozo denied a woman's case against the Long Island Railroad Co.

One opinion arising from the actions of this class of people included a Warren Burger concurrence that quotes Blackstone describing a "crime not fit to be named." This class of people was the subject of Colorado's Amendment 2, which made it illegal for the government to enact legislation prohibiting them from discrimination, thus leading to the case of Romer v. Evans. Name this class of people at the center of Bowers v. Hardwick and Lawrence v. Texas, which concerned their right to engage in sodomy.

This practice cannot singlehandedly stand in for free will in certain circumstances according to Brown v. Illinois. Michigan v. Tucker held that failure to conduct this practice did not invoke the fruit of the poisonous tree doctrine, though the Court may re-rule on that issue in light of a case holding that this practice stems from a constitutional rule, Dickerson v. United States.This practice is the result of a case in which the Supreme Court held that procedural safeguards must be in place before prosecutors can use evidence obtained during custodial interrogation. Name this practice in which a suspect is informed of various rights, including the right to remain silent.

This case created a cause of action that led to the case that extended Twombly v. Bell Atlantic, the landmark pleading case Ashcroft v. Iqbal. The cause of action created by this case is similar to that arising from the Civil Rights Act of 1871. Name this 1971 case in which the Supreme Court found that the Fourth Amendment implies a namesake cause of action against the federal government, and whose defendants are amusingly listed as Six Unknown Federal Narcotics Agents.
Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents

This thinker's ideas were popularized by a contemporary in an article for the Atlantic Monthly that also originated the nickname "Libyan Sibyl" for this thinker. This thinker repeatedly expressed support for "keeping the thing going while things are stirring" in an address to the American Equal Rights Association. One speech by this thinker repeats the question "Where did your Christ come from?" and mentions "this thing in the head" called "intellect." The printed text of that speech delivered by this thinker was notably altered in a later publication by Frances Dana Barker Gage, who inserted its title question four times, including after this thinker's declaration that "I could work as much and eat as much as a manÂ—when I could get itÂ—and bear the lash as well!" name this former slave and women's rights advocate, best known for delivering a speech later given the title "Ain't I A Woman?"

Following the work of Eric Hobsbawm, Nathan Brown described the "invention of banditry" in this nation, in his article "Brigands and State Building." A historian from this modern-day country wrote an open letter criticizing a population who "rebelled against their sultan six years ago," and wrote the Remarkable Remnants of Lives and Events. An object from this country provided the basis for the Letter to Monsieur Dacier, and was the subject of a lengthy "Description" produced by a group of so-called "savants" at the beginning of the nineteenth century. The best-known book by the historian Timothy Mitchell is titled Colonising. This country was the home of the historian Abd al-Rahman al-Jabarti. An analysis of a 1910 speech by Lord Balfour is presented alongside a history of this country written by Lord Cromer in the first chapter of Edward Said's Orientalism. Thomas Young and Jean-Francois Champollion rivaled over the transliteration of a script from this modern-day country. Name this modern-day country, which was the subject of increased European interest after Napoleon invaded it and found the Rosetta Stone.

This historical era's "frame of mind" titles a book by Walter Houghton, who curated a notable "Wellesley Index" of primary sources from this period. The historiography of the fatal beating of a gingerbread vendor during this historical era exemplifies the transition from "facts of the past" to "facts of history," according to a book by E.H. Carr. Caroll Smith-Rosenberg's Disorderly Conduct is a collection of essays about this historical era. A book by Mike Davis studying the connections between the El NiÃ±o-Southern Oscillation and world famine is titled for the "holocausts" of the later part of this historical era.The introduction to a famously inaccurate historical work about this era includes the caveat "Je n'impose rien; jene propose rien; j'expose." Cardinal Manning and Thomas Arnold are two of the title "eminent" figures from thisera in a book by Lytton Strachey. Name this lengthy historical era of the BritishEmpire named for a female monarch.

Warning: specific term required.A description of one of these entities is the only Aristotelian text to have been recovered since the Renaissance. In another treatise, Aristotle noted that, since most places do not have the resources to make every person happy, one must theorize about the non-ideal kinds of these entities, since they are the only ones that will be actually used. Book Six of Polybius's Histories classified a Roman entity of this kind as "mixed," which leads Scipio to call it the best one in a later dialogue. A six-part classification of these entities is based on the distinction between "proper" and "perverted" senses of justice. A revised one of these entities is proposed in Book Three of Cicero's De Legibus. These entities are the formal cause of the polis, according to Aristotle. Aristotle's Politics classifies tyrannies, oligarchies, and democracies as what kind of entity, examples of which were written by Lycurgus and Solon?

An article by William Appleman Williams connects this idea to a foreign policy advocated by Brooks Adams. The essay which originated this idea expresses agreement with Achille Loria's idea that the study of economic development is aided through the study of colonial life. The "populist" and "progressive" strains of this idea are discussed by Richard Slotkin in the final book of a trilogy which began with the books Regeneration Through Violence and The Fatal Environment. William Cronon argued that this idea was insufficiently connected to the development of markets in his book Nature's Metropolis. The paper that originated this idea was written following the 1890 census, and claims that the "existence of an area of free land, its continuous recession, and the advance of American settlement" explains the development of American democracy. Name this idea developed by Frederick Jackson Turner in a paper titled for its namesake boundary's "significance" in American history.

Shortly after this Supreme Court case was decided, Katherine Franke scathingly reviewed the languageused in its majority opinion in a Columbia Law Review article titled for this case's "domesticated liberty."An amicus brief filed in this case challenged Warren Burger's assertion in an earlier case that classifying acertain act as a fundamental right "would be to cast aside millennia of moral teaching," and was written by agroup of historians including John D'Emilio, Nancy Cott, and George Chauncey. The majority opinion inthis case claimed that the legal basis for an earlier case had since been eroded by decisions in Planned Parenthoodv. Casey and Romer v. Evans. This 2003 decision overturned Bowers v. Hardwick. Name thisSupreme Court case that mandated the legalization of same-sex sexual activity throughout the U.S.

In A Most Dangerous Book, Christopher Krebs argued that an ethnographic work by this writer helped to define the core concepts of Nazism. Justus Lipsius relied heavily on this writer in penning his Six Books of Politics, and prepared an edition of this writer's work for Maximilian II. In the introduction to one of his works, this writer described his style as "sine ira et studio." Giuseppe Toffanin divided Renaissance interpreters of this writer into two camps: thinkers like Leonardo Bruni who employed him in support of Republican ideals, and thinkers who used him as a proxy for supporting Machiavelli. Those are the so- called "red" and "black" political interpreters of this writer. This writer's first historical work was a biography of his father-in-law's governorship of Roman Britain. Name this Roman historian who wrote the Agricola and the Annals.

Although he wasn't French, this thinker's first major work was a defence of the érudits against the philosophes, and was titled Essay on the Study of Literature. The last chapter of this thinker's most famous work contrasts the "sacrilege" of Paul III's nephews with the "liberality" of Benedict XIV, who consecrated the Colosseum. This historian's most famous work was criticized for beginning too late, and thus giving too much credit to external factors, by Arnold J. Toynbee. That work by this historian was challenged by Henri Pirenne's most famous thesis. This historian calculated that the number of early martyrs was far lower than the Church claimed, and argued that paganism was in fact quite tolerant. That work by this historian was one of the first to draw mainly on primary sources, and argues that its title event was the result of a decline in civic virtue due to the rise of Christianity. Name this English historian who wrote Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire.

This author traced the use of youth-abbeys as rites of passage in the essay "The Reasons of Misrule. Another essay by this author claims certain Catholic religious riots were more violent due to a desire to "purify" the body social. This author interviewed Toni Morrison for a book that analyzes films like Gillo Pontecorvo's Burn! And Stanley Kubrick's Spartacus. This author relied on pardon tales recounted in letters of remission to write the book Fiction in the Archives. This historian more recently authored a controversial biography of the Moroccan traveler Leo Africanus, titled Trickster Travels. The best-known book by this historian claims that the wife of the title legless veteran of the Italian Wars conspired to replace him with the imposter Arnaud de Tilh during his absence. Name this American historian best known for her work on early modern France, including The Return of Martin Guerre.

This man was asked, "where is our breakfast" by protesters during a bread riot. This ruler promoted the "revolution of rectification" policy, and his October Paper outlined his program of al-intifah or "opening", which allowed foreign banks back into his country. He was survived by his popular wife Jehan, and his ostentation led to his subjects to call him "Faruq II". This man was celebrated for "the crossing", where his armies broke through the Bar Lev line at the beginning of the October War. Jimmy Carter mediated an agreement between this man and Menachem Begin at Camp David. Name this successor to Gamal Abdel Nasser.

In a popular contemporary pasquinade, this man was attacked for traveling with "Two Turks, three Whores, and a half-dozen nurses." Both Thomas Hanmer and William Bromley refused to take office under this man, whose supporters consolidated their position by instituting the Septennial Act, which allowed for seven years between elecitons. The first half of this king's reign was dominated by the ministry of James Stanhope, who negotiated the Triple Alliance for this king over the objections of Robert Walpole. This man's accession was made possible by the 1701 Act of Settlement, which ensured a Protestant king over the claims of James, the Old Pretender. Identify this king who in 1714 succeeded Queen Anne and founded England's Hanoverian dynasty.

Robert Boyle left funds for one of these institutions to be established at Bafferton Hall under the auspices of William & Mary. Richard Pratt led the large-scale founding of these in the 1880s, declaring an intent to "save the man." These institutions were the subject of the 1928 Meriam Report, which recommended abolition of the Uniform Course of Study and a raising of the minimum age for enrollment. These places "made me learn your white man rule, be a fool" according to a protest song by a singer who was sent to one at age five in North Dakota. Pop Warner was coaching at one of these institutions, known as Carlisle, while Jim Thorpe was enrolled. Name these BIA-run boarding institutions which attempted to remove Native American culture from children.

This officer first attracted attention at Gamaizieh and Toski, where he defeated bands of dervishes. This person was about to depose Abbas II as Khedive when he was recalled. Earlier, his power struggle for the Indian army ended with the resignation of Lord Curzon. In one assignment, this man supplanted Frederick Sleigh Roberts as commander-in-chief and used a blockhouse network, concentration camps, and the burning of farms to subjugate his opponents. This man's forces met those of Jean-Baptiste Marchand at Fashoda, shortly after he defeated the Mahdists at Omdurman. Name this symbol of the British military who was featured on World War I recruiting posters before being killed at sea by a German mine (MINE).

Article 82 of this legislation prevented political assemblies from meeting at Saumur. The second of two brevets passed after this legislation provided a royal subsidy of 180,000 ecus a year to pay for garrisons. People and towns exempt from this legislation were outlined in its 56 "secret articles", and it took 10 years for the Parlement of Rouen to ratify it. After its policies were ended, the Edict of Potsdam of was issued. This document made Catholicism the state religion, but was overturned in the Edict of Fontainebleau. Name this document issued by Henry IV that granted religious toleration to French Huguenots.

Battles in this conflict included two back-to-back engagements at Siping. This conflict saw the April 12 Incident, and the victorious army in this conflict was instructed to follow the Three Rules of Discipline and Eight Points for Attention. This war was fictionalized in Andre Malraux's novel Man's Fate. This war saw the Battle of Luding Bridge and the Pingjin Campaign. George Marshall was sent to Yen-an to try to mediate an end to this conflict. One side departed from Jiangxi in the Long March. Name this war between the Kuomintang and the Communist Party of a certain Asian nation.

One member of this family became the grand constable of Naples after being summoned by King Ladislas. In addition to Muzio Attendolo, this family included a man who allied with Maximilian I and Charles VIII of France against Ferdinand I of Spain after deposing his nephew, Gian Galeazzo; that man's sons were later defeated at Marignano. Another member of this family won the Battle of Anghiari against a city that he gained control of on the death of Filippo Maria. That member of this family won the dukedom in the Treaty of Lodi, which ended the war between this family's stronghold and Venice, and was followed by a member dubbed "il Moro." Including the mercenary Francesco and his son Ludovico, identify this family which supplanted the Visconti in Milan.

A memoir about being raised in this family is Prison and Chocolate Cake. A woman with this maiden name served successively as ambassador to the Soviet Union and the United States from 1947 to 1951. Though it is not the Fords, a man with this last name founded the newspaper The Independent in 1919 and wrote a namesake "report" advocating a constitutional dominion, five years after co-founding the Swaraj Party. Another person with this last name called for Western support during a border war with China, ending his stated policy of nonalignment. Name this family, including Motilal and the first Indian prime minister, Jawaharlal.

A report sympathetic to the people targeted in this event was issued by the McGucken Commission. The first lady was accused of "Blindly Race Discord" for an editorial she wrote condemning this event. Prior to this event, seventeen of the namesake group of people were identified as being "biologically inclined toward criminality" in the Sleepy Lagoon trial. This event began when some men claimed to have been robbed by a group of pachucos and was ended when the War Department forbade entry into certain barrios. Name these 1943 riots in Los Angeles where servicemen attacked Latinos wearing the namesake type of clothing.

This man's son lost his Persian Gulf holdings when Ilumailu founded the First Sea-Land Dynasty. This father of Shamshuiluna defeated Zimrilim in order to destroy Mari, and he ruled during the time when the Akkadian language displaced the Sumerian and worship of Enlil was replaced with worship of Marduk. He overran Isin and Elam before making his great conquest of Larsa in 1699 BCE. This king may be best known for a stele found in 1901 CE which orders the death of the builder if a house kills the owner, and modifies punishments based on membership in one of three social classes. Name this Babylonian ruler who promulgated the oldest surviving law code.

During this man's rule, his country's first newspaper, Records, debuted. The posad joined in the unsuccessful Astrakhan Revolt against this monarch, who named Franz Lefort as one of three "Grand Ambassadors." He eliminated the distinction between hereditary and granted lands, and he mandated primogeniture. He also reformed the civil service with the Table of Ranks and founded the city of Taganrog after fighting alongside Austria, Venice, and Poland in the Holy League and capturing Azov. Following several revolts, he disbanded the streltsy. This ruler worked undercover in a Dutch East India Company shipyard and instituted a beard tax. Name this modernizing tsar of Russia who founded a "window on the west" on the Baltic that bears his name.

A 1960 law to accomplish this action was advanced by Venezuela's Romulo Betancourt, who hoped that it would discourage the migratory "conuqueros." The Argentinian leader Bernardino Rivadavia was called the "patron saint" of this action, and promulgated a law based on the Roman concept of emphyteusis. The Castro government in 1959 passed a law which performed this action, giving every peasant family two caballerias and stripping the United Fruit Company of its properties. Generally tageted at latifundia and haciendas, identify this type of action carried out in many Latin American nations, which sought a more equitable distribution of a certain immovable resource.

They're not the LARF, but this group fractured following the assassination of Leamon Hunt, the director of the peace keeping force in Sinai. This group emerged from the Metropolitan Political Collective. Many of its members were offered protection by the Mitterand Doctrine. During this group's "Winter of Fire" campaign, they kidnapped NATO Brigadier General James Dozier. Their most infamous victim was found in the trunk of a Renault 4. Eight members of this group were exchanged for a prosecutor named Mario Sossi. Name this group that in 1978 kidnapped and killed Christian Democrat leader Aldo Moro, the Prime Minister of Italy.

The outlines of this organization were set down at the Council of Troyes. This organization was given the Isle of Lundy by King John, during whose rule it was headed by Amaric de St. Its privileges were confirmed by the papal bull Omne datum optimum of Innocent II. This organization, founded by Hugh de Payens, was largely eliminated due to the machinations of Clement V and Philip the Fair, the latter of whom, in 1307, ordered the arrest of every member of this organization including Jacques de Molay, its last leader. Identify this religious military order, originally established during the Crusades for the ostensible purpose of protecting pilgrims to the Holy Land.

Eight months after this large battle, another attempt to take its namesake town was made at Hobkirk's Hill, after which it was burned and abandoned. As at Guilford Courthouse, James Webster led the decisive troop movement in this battle, which began under the temporary commander Lord Rawdon. One army in this battle had just changed commanders after the capture of Benjamin Lincoln and was marching south from Hillsboro. Prussian general Johann de Kalb was mortally wounded at this battle, which led to Nathanael Greene taking command in the South. Charles Cornwallis defeated Horatio Gates at what August 16, 1780 battle in South Carolina?

According to the architect of these laws, the assassination of the Duke of Berry at the Paris Opera House "could not have better eulogized [them]". Bernard Bolzanno lost his teaching position as a result of these laws, while Wilhelm von Humboldt resigned from a government post in protest. They were passed after the murder of August Kotzebue by Karl Sand, and they established a committee in Mainz to investigate "demagogues". These laws broke up the burschenschaften student groups, and imposed wider press censorship. Name these laws promoted by Carl Metternich in 1819 that sought to repress liberalism in the German states.

One of these places was discovered by Johann Schneider and reconstructed in Borg. A heart and swastika mosaic was found in the triclinium of one of these places named Lullingstone. An example of an elegant domus in one of these places can be found at Settefinestre. E. M. Schtaerman distinguishes these places from latifundia by their being owned by lesser nobility. One of these places contained the Furietti Centaurs and the Canopus garden; that UNESCO World Heritage Site was built by Hadrian in Tivoli. Many of these places had lodging for the slaves that harvested the wine. Name these Roman country estates.

At one point, the Argives established a base on Cythera for the purpose of recruiting these people to conduct raids. According to Thucydides, a war against these people was triggered by the Thasos revolt and lasted ten years. The neaodamodeis were a group of these people recruited for hoplite service. These people were subject to oversight by a police force known as the Krypteia, and after returning from Colonae, the general Pausanias was charged with a plot to engineer an uprising of these people. Upon entering office, ephors would symbolically declare war on these people, who may have been the original inhabitants of Laconia before the Doric invasion. Including the subjugated population of Messenia, identify these state slaves of Sparta.

This group was attacked by the Worthing-based periodical, The Skeleton. The head of this organization is elected by the High Council, and leaders have included Edward Higgins. Many of its songs were composed by George Scott Railton, while James Barker printed its periodical, The War Cry. Its founder was once described leading "bull-necked convicts" and "vermin-eaten saints with mouldy breath"; that same work repeatedly asks, "Are you washed in the blood of the Lamb?" and was written by Vachel Lindsay. Founded by William Booth, name this charitable organization that collects donations during the Christmas season.

This woman paid for Edith How-Martyn to operate in England and personally financed a Zurich successor to the Geneva Population Conference. Through Katharine McCormick, she secured funding for Gregory Pincus's research. The principles of an organization she founded were outlined in The Pivot of Civilization. She helped overturn obscenity laws in U.S. V. One Package of Japanese Pessaries, although six issues of her The Woman Rebel were banned for obscenity. A cause advocated by this author of "What Every Girl Should Know" was achieved through Griswold v. Connecticut. Name this birth control advocate.

Critics attacked the access that the American James Hausman had to this leader. In 1919, this future Princeton graduate was elected president of the exile KPG government. He fled to Hawaii after the April 19 Revolution. Earlier, this husband of Franziska Donner secured a treason conviction for Progressive Party leader Cho Bong Am. Jimmie Leach observed his crackdown of the April 3rd uprising on Jeju Island. In one war, this man fled his capital, leaving its citizens to the mercy of KPA forces attacking from above the 38th parallel. He was president during the Inchon Landing. Name this first president of the Republic of Korea.

One book about this event includes a poem subtitled "A Requiem," which tells of how "skimming lightly, wheeling still, the swallows fly low." Another poem about this event describes a "flag whose stars, like planets strike us through," and is titled "The Frenzy in the Wake." This event is the subject of a 43-poem cycle which opens by describing how "the white tents cluster in camps," and includes a poem in which the narrator describes "A procession winding around me, solemn sweet and slow," titled "By the Bivouac's Fitful Flame." Literature about this event was the subject of Edmund Wilson's Patriotic Gore. The subject of Herman Melville's Battle Pieces, identify this event, the subject of a section of Leaves of Grass titled Drum Taps.

This policy was the basis for a constitutional amendment drafted by Thomas Jefferson in 1803 but never proposed to Congress. One agreement for implementing this policy was negotiated by John Eaton and John Coffee; that was the Treaty of Pontotoc. Another attempt to implement this policy took place when one party to an 1825 treaty executed its signer, William McIntosh, which the other party to that treaty took to be an abrogation of it. Perhaps the most famous instantiation of this policy came via an 1830 piece of legislation which provided for the government's authority to sign the Treaty of New Echota and force a certain population to take the Trail of Tears. Identify this US government policy of relocating Native Americans to western territories.

One group of people engaged in this activity was the Order of the Lone Star, which drafted John Quitman as leader. That group was comprised of disciples of a man who was executed following the Battle of Las Pozas for engaging in this activity. Perhaps the most prominent man engaged in this activity gave expropriated property to Cornelius Garrison and Charles Morgan after being financed by the Accessory Transit Company of Cornelius Vanderbilt. That practitioner of this activity was ultimately executed in Honduras, three years after being deposed as president of Nicaragua. Identify this activity practiced by Narciso Lopez and William Walker, which consisted of foreign adventurers, usually backed by slavery interests, attempting to take over Latin American states.

A Supreme Court Justice with this last name argued that an Indiana military trial was illegal in the majority opinion in Ex parte Milligan. Along with Bandemer, a man with this surname was a party to a 1986 Supreme Court case that upheld the practice of political gerrymandering. A man with this surname had a $100,000 bail bond partially paid by Horace Greeley. This surname was shared by Charles W. Bryan's Democratic running mate in 1924. A president with this surname was elected on a ticket with Alexander Stephens. Give this surname shared by the first and only President of the Confederacy.

Before becoming Abraham Lincoln's Secretary of War, Edwin Stanton served in this cabinet position under James Buchanan. A man who held this post under FDR led the effort to ban gold clauses in contracts. Besides Homer Cummings, Mrs. Mabel Willebrandt was appointed assistant to this post by Warren Harding, serving under Harry M. Daugherty and tasked with supervising Prohibition. One holder of this post deported over 200 people on the Buford after conducting the Palmer Raids. The first woman to hold this position ordered the seizure of Elian Gonzalez and was named Janet Reno. Name this "chief lawyer" of the United States.

This man was impressed by a farmer who pledged to pay "ten percent of his aches and pains" and exempted the farmer from further taxes. He organized the "Hillsmen" in order to break the two-party dominance of the Plain and Coast factions. This man approved of the elder Militiades's plan to seize Chersonesus. He acquired riches from the Pangaeum mines in order to hire men to fight for him at Pallene. During his rule, the Hall of the Mysteries and Propylaea were built. After attracting attention by capturing the harbor of Megara, this man attacked several of his mules and slashed his own flesh in order to be allowed a club-bearing bodyguard. His house's rule was ended when Harmodius and Aristogeiton killed his son Hipparchus. Name this three-time tyrant of Athens.

Agents of this country attempted to poison the drink of dissident Paul Goma in Paris, only for Goma's drink to be spilled by an undercover French agent. This country's dictatorship was opposed by the "Letter of the Six." An August 1969 trip to this country by Richard Nixon was the first time a U.S. President visited a Communist state. The Groz faction in this country launched a purge of Jews and Soviet-sympathizing "Muscovites," who were led by Ana Pauker. Another of its leaders doubled down on censorship with the July Theses and took the title of "Conducator;" that man, whose regime was enforced by the Securitate, succeeded Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej. Name this country where a Christmas 1989 revolution executed its last Communist dictator, Nicolae Ceausescu.

This ruler used bribery to net himself four votes for the title of Holy Roman Emperor, which he claimed by descent from Philip of Swabia, over the three garnered by Richard of Cornwall, but the election was vetoed by Alexander IV. James the Conqueror helped this man suppress a rebellion. Under this ruler's supervision, a legal code called the Seven Divisions of the Law was assembled. It was for this king that Jehuda ben Moses Cohen and Isaac ben Sid assembled namesake astronomical tables. This king legally recognized the sheep ranching society called the Mesta, and his court scholars produced the history Premera cronica general. Succeeded by his son Sancho IV, identify this ruler of Castile and Leon from 1252 to 1284, renowned for his alleged sagacity.

This speech's final paragraph announces, "neither let us be slandered from our duty by false accusations against us, nor frightened from it by menaces of destruction to the Government". Elsewhere, this oration examined restrictions placed on Tennessee's entrance to the Union. This oration was originally to be given at Henry Ward Beecher's church. It argued that at least 21 of the 39 Framers advocated controlling or abolishing slavery, a statement that refuted a claim made in an earlier address by the speaker's rival, Stephen A. Douglas. Name this 1859 address given at a namesake New York school by Abraham Lincoln.

This man founded the ILO at Versailles after supporting Woodrow Wilson throughout the war. With his ally Adolph Strasser, this man successfully campaigned to abolish the tenement system of production and began the "blue label" campaign for union-made goods. The Supreme Court voided this man's conviction for violating an injunction in the Bucks Stove and Range Company case. This advocate of "voluntarism" joined the Anti-Imperialist League out of fear that cheap Filipino labor would flood the west coast. Earlier, this cigar-maker led fellow craft unionists out of the Knights of Labor in 1886. Name this British-born founder of the American Federation of Labor.

Reformer Lucy Page Gaston is sometimes called the Carrie Nation of this industry. Milanese patriots started boycotting this industry on January 1st, 1848, leading to a namesake riot. This industry conducted Operation Berkshire, and proceeds from this industry fund the American Legacy Foundation. Lowell Bergman's interview of an executive in this industry named Jeffrey Wigand was dramatized in a 1999 Michael Mann film. In the US, companies in this industry agreed to the Master Settlement Agreement in 1998 that partially funds The Truth campaigns. Name this industry whose products contain nicotine.

A subject of this king was attacked in the papal bull Unigenitus; that man was Pasquier Quesnel. During his reign, Henri Philippe de Chauvelin helped secure the expulsion of the Jesuits. This king tried to place the father of his wife Marie Leszczy?ska on the Polish throne. He survived an assassination attempt by Robert Damiens, and his finance minister John Law presided over the Mississippi Bubble. One of this man's mistresses uttered the famous line, "after us, the deluge" and was named Madame de Pompadour. Under this ruler, France lost the Seven Years' War. Name this man who ruled as King of France from 1715-1774.

This battle saw the death of a man who had previously defeated Severus in a civil war. A monument commemorating this battle includes scenes of the victor's earlier Siege of Verona. The losing commander moved his troops to a plain near Saxa Rubra after receiving a bad omen in the Sibylline Books. That losing commander's head was shipped to Carthage to prove that he drowned during this battle. The victor at this battle later issued the Edict of Milan because he reportedly saw "in this sign conquer" written on a flaming cross prior to this battle. Name this battle where Maxentius was defeated by Constantine the Great.

One holder of this office used a string attached to a shotgun to kill himself after breakfast. The first holder of this office signed the Solemn Public Act, only emigrated from Pennsylvania after losing his inheritance to his brother in a boxing match, and won election to this office in a landslide over explorer William Clark. Another holder of this office issued Executive Order 44, known as the Extermination Order, against Mormons. In addition to Alexander McNair and Lillburn Boggs, this office was held for most of the 1990s by a man who died in a 2000 plane crash while running for the Senate against another former holder of this office, who anointed himself with Crisco upon winning it. Name this state executive office, held by Mel Carnahan and John Ashcroft.

This king had Richard Scrope, archbishop of York, executed for conspiring with the duke of Northumberland to rebel. Together with Thomas Mowbray, this man led an opposition group called the lords appellants. During his last days, his court was split between factions loyal to his successor and those loyal to Thomas Arundel, archbishop of Canterbury. This king's achievements included the suppression of the Owen Glendower rebellion early in his rule, as well as the defeat of a rebellion raised by Henry Percy, the earl of Northumberland known as Hotspur. The eldest surviving son of John of Gaunt, identify this king who succeeded his cousin Richard II, the first of three Lancastrian kings of England.

This man once brought a sack of fraudulent ballots before the U.S. Senate to demonstrate that William Vare's election as Senator was crooked. In one Senate election, Boies Penrose defeated both future Red Scare orchestrator A. Mitchell Palmer and this man. This man's open letter to Senator Jonathan Dolliver of Iowa led to the climax of a scandal he was involved in, which began when Morgan and Guggenheim's "Alaska Syndicate" was accused of corruption by Louis Glavis. This man, who served two nonconsecutive terms as Governor of Pennsylvania beginning in 1923 and 1931, was fired by William Howard Taft after clashing with Secretary of the Interior Richard Ballinger. Name this Progressive icon, an active chief of the U.S. Forest Service.

During the Clodius-Milo controversy, this tribune of the plebeians delivered a series of speeches condemning Cicero. Dio Cassius relates that this man was expelled from the Senate following the publication of an anonymous "Invective against" this man, which claimed that he had used ill-gotten wealth to create some eponymous gardens. After being designated praetor, this man unsuccessfully attempted to suppress a rebellion among Caesar's troops and was given the governorship of Africa Nova. After retirement from politics, he composed his most famous works, the first of which was an analysis of the Catiline conspiracy and the second of which was a history of the rebellion of Masinissa's grandson. Identify this Roman historian of The Jugurthine War.

In 1919, Charles Ruthenberg was involved in a Cleveland riot on this holiday. This holiday was traditionally the date on which tenants in New York City would switch residences. Yale graduates like Phillip Dean and Gordon Sterrett prepare for the Gamma Psi dance in New York City in an F. Scott Fitzgerald story named for this holiday. This day is officially Loyalty Day in the United States, while in Germany the eve of this holiday is celebrated as Walpurgis Night. Fertility ceremonies are held in England on this day, which is also celebrated as International Workers' Day. Name this spring holiday where a pole is erected.

This campaign was the subject of Jacob Van Staaveren's history titled Gradual Failure and it was overseen by Ulysses Sharp, who urged for its intensification. A key technology in this campaign was the MSQ-77 system, which made it possible to avoid bad weather, and this campaign included a subsidiary operation called Iron Hand. After proceeding in two-week cycles, this campaign was interrupted for 37 days to allow for negotiations, which included 14 points by Dean Rusk. This campaign commenced in full after 31 Americans were killed at Pleiku and Qui Nhon, and concluded shortly following the lifting of the siege of Khe Sanh during the Tet Offensive. Identify this military campaign of the Vietnam war which deployed air power to bomb North Vietnam.

One legend about this battle holds that a solider threw a giant boulder at the feet of the winning commander prior to it, thereby "casting his vote" against retreat. In the aftermath of this battle, victorious commander negotiated a deal with Thebes whereby the Thebans handed over those who were sympathetic to this battle's loing side. Despite the long preliminaries to this battle, the Eleans and Mantineans still managed to arrive after it ended. Taking place simultaneously with the triumph of Leotychidas over Tigranes at the battle of Mycale, this battle saw the defeat and death of Mardonius at the hands of a force led by the Spartan general Pausanias. Identify this 479 BCE battle of the Greco-Persian wars, which ended Xerxes I's campaign.

This leader labeled wealthy citizens who could import fruit from abroad as "banana eaters". He spearheaded the Great Manmade River, and forces under this man fought a southern neighbor in the Toyota War. This man came to power by overthrowing a monarch who descended from the founder of the Senussi movement. During a speech at the UN, he once tossed the UN Charter on the floor, while he espoused an Islamic-based socialism in his Green Book. Agents of this man orchestrated the bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland. Ousted by a rebel group based in Benghazi, name this recently deposed ruler of Libya.

This man was a leading speaker at the Urbana and Chillicothe councils. After going on a raid with his adoptive father Blackfish, he excoriated his colleagues for burning a white man at the stake. He became leader of his band after the death at Nashville of his brother Cheeseekau, and was chosen to lead the attack on Fort Recovery. He led a large army from Fort Malden that helped the British capture Detroit. This ally of Henry Proctor and opponent of the "Peace Chiefs" gained further popularity when his brother received a vision from the "Master of Life." name this man who lost the Battle of the Thames to William Henry Harrison and was the brother of "The Prophet."

Warning that the first of these events, sometimes called the Bun'ei one, was about to occur came from rebels in the nation that provided most of the materiel for these events. The plan for another of these events was to join the Easter Route Division to the Chiang-nan Division. One of these events saw a military force occupying the Hizen province and forcing a retreat by forces under the command of Shoni Sukeyoshi, while another of these events saw most of 140,000 soldiers under the general Hung Ch'a-ch'iu killed after the destruction of their ships. Thwarted twice in 1274 and 1281 by the destruction of a fleet at Hakata Bay by a kamikaze, or typhoon, identify these military campaigns undertaken by the Yuan dynasty to subjugate an island nation.

Until the 1960s, control of this country alternated between the descendants of Jaber and Salem. An airport in this country was bombed in 1983 by Jamal Jafaar Mohammed and the al-Da'wah group. In Operation Vantage, the British protected this newly independent country from the aggression of Abd al-Karim Qasim. Emirs of this country from the al-Sabah dynasty include Mubarak the Great, and it was founded by the Anaiza clans who migrated from the Najd region. Its alleged practice of slant drilling prompted a foreign invasion by a Ba'ath leader, which itself prompted Operation Desert Shield. Name this country invaded in 1990 by Iraq.

This city was the home to "The Man Who Sold America", ad-man Albert D. Lasker. Over 600 Hawthorne Works employees died when the Eastland capsized in a river outside of this city. Another 600 people of this city died in a fire at the "absolutely fireproof" Iroquois Theater in 1903. Home to mayors Jane Byrne and Harold Washington, the original Ferris Wheel was built for an event in this city supervised by Daniel Burnham and chronicled in Erik Larson's The Devil in the White City. Name this Midwestern city which experienced a Great Fire in 1871, also home to the Daley political machine.

This war included a successful siege of Lille prosecuted by Francois de Crequi, and the outbreak of this war caused the invaded polity to enter into a Triple Alliance with Sweden and England via the Treaty of Breda. This war was essentially a complete victory for forces led by the Marshal de Turenne, and before the treaty ending it was signed, the Prince de Conde captured the Franche-Comte. This conflict had its origin in one king's claim that, since Spain had failed to pay Marie-Therese's dowry, her renunciation of Dutch possessions was void and they thus belonged to her husband. Identify this war waged in 1667 by Louis XIV against Charles II to gain the Spanish Netherlands, which was ended with the 1668 Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle.

Arnold Amaury, a veteran of the Cathar Crusade, chronicled this battle. Prior to this battle, French forces commanded by Diego Lopez de Haro slaughtered all but three of the inhabitants of Malagon. In the aftermath of this battle, the victorious commander seized Ubeda and Baeza. Innocent III convinced some veterans of the Fourth Crusade to campaign with the winning side in this battle, whose commanders included Sancho VII of Navarre. This battle was a defeat for Muhammad al-Nasir. Name this 1212 victory for Christian armies under the command of Alfonso VIII of Castille over the Almohads in Spain.
Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa

Supporters of this man wore red badges reading "Federation or Death", and this runaway gained his wealth working in the saladero industry. His wife, Doña Encarnación, led the Revolution of the Restorers. His government was opposed by the unitarios, and he fought the Battle of Vuelta de Obligado in reaction to a French blockade of his country's chief port during the War of the Confederation. This ruler controlled a secret police force called the mazorca. This man fell from power when Justo Jose de Urquiza defeated his forces at the Battle of Caseros. Name this man who ruled as a dictator from 1835-1852 in Argentina.
